subject: Banking
title: Why Banks Keep Failing
description: A 60-second lesson on Why Banks Keep Failing.

hook.text: Banks have failed for 4,000 years. The causes repeat: excess leverage, risky bets, fraud, and loss of public confidence.

buildup.text: Every banking crisis follows a pattern: innovation, euphoria, over-lending, then collapse. The cycle never breaks.

discovery.text: Humans are wired for short-term thinking. Bankers optimize for this quarter's profit, not the next decade's stability.

twist.text: Regulations written after each crisis get weakened during the next boom. Memory fades, rules relax, and risk returns.

climax.text: Banking failures are systemic, not accidental. The incentive structure rewards risk-taking until the system breaks.

punchline.text: Same causes for 4,000 years. Leverage, risk, fraud, and lost trust.

quiz.question: Why do banking crises keep repeating?
options: Structural incentives reward risk-taking, and regulations weaken over time

details.summary: Banks keep failing because their fundamental business model of borrowing short and lending long creates an inherent fragility. Combined with leverage, confidence-dependent funding, and human tendency to underestimate risk, failures are inevitable.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding why bank failures are structurally inevitable rather than merely the result of bad actors helps set realistic expectations for regulation and prepares society for the next inevitable crisis.
takeaways: Maturity transformation, borrowing short to lend long, creates inherent fragility
Bank leverage amplifies small asset losses into existential capital shortfalls
Every generation believes it has finally solved the problem of bank failures

faq.question: Why is the bank business model inherently risky?
faq.answer: Banks fund long-term loans with short-term deposits that can be withdrawn at any time. This maturity mismatch means that even a perfectly managed bank can fail if enough depositors demand their money simultaneously.

faq.question: Can narrow banking prevent bank failures?
faq.answer: Narrow banking, where deposits are backed entirely by safe government securities, would eliminate the risk but also eliminate bank lending. It would be safer but would require a completely different system for channeling credit to businesses and consumers.
